papers.title: Generative AI Engineering: Large Language Models and Intelligent Agents
papers.abstract: developments in contemporary computing, transforming the way intelligent systems understand information, generate content, reason over knowledge, interact with users, and perform complex tasks. The rapid evolution of Large Language Models, multimodal foundation models, retrieval-augmented generation, intelligent agents, and autonomous workflows has created a new generation of AI systems that extend beyond conventional prediction and classification. These developments are influencing software engineering, scientific research, healthcare, education, business, robotics, cybersecurity, manufacturing, and many other domains. The book Generative AI Engineering: Large Language Models and Intelligent Agents has been developed to provide a comprehensive academic and engineering-oriented treatment of these emerging technologies. The book approaches Generative AI not merely as a collection of models or tools, but as an engineering discipline involving model architecture, data and knowledge integration, prompting, retrieval, agent orchestration, evaluation, security, deployment, optimization, and responsible operation. The objective is to provide readers with both conceptual foundations and a practical understanding of how modern Generative AI systems are designed and integrated into intelligent applications. The book begins with the foundations of Generative AI and Large Language Models. Chapter 1, Foundations of Generative AI and Large Language Models, introduces the evolution of generative modeling from statistical Natural Language Processing to modern foundation models and LLMs. It examines the distinction between discriminative and generative learning and provides a detailed treatment of Transformer architecture, self-attention, multi-head attention, positional encoding, embeddings, and encoder–decoder architectures. The chapter further explores LLM pre-training, next-token prediction, supervised fine-tuning, instruction tuning, parameter-efficient fine-tuning, tokenization, contextual representations, prompting, context engineering, inference optimization, quantization, and model ecosystems. Applications in intelligent tutoring, software engineering, healthcare, scientific knowledge discovery, business intelligence, and customer support establish the practical relevance of LLMs. Chapter 2, LLM Engineering, Retrieval-Augmented Generation, and Multimodal Intelligence, moves from model fundamentals toward application engineering. It explains how LLM APIs, model-serving architectures, prompt templates, structured outputs, function calling, and schema-constrained generation can be integrated into production applications. Particular emphasis is given to Retrieval-Augmented Generation, including document ingestion, chunking, retrieval, reranking, grounding, and knowledge-intensive generation. Advanced retrieval techniques such as hybrid search, dense retrieval, query expansion, query decomposition, graph-based retrieval, and agentic retrieval are examined. The chapter also discusses vector databases, metadata filtering, knowledge graphs, multimodal foundation models, multimodal embeddings, fine-tuning, LoRA, continual adaptation, orchestration frameworks, memory management, and production-oriented architectures. Applications in enterprise knowledge systems, healthcare, scientific research, legal and financial analysis, education, manufacturing, and intelligent search demonstrate the breadth of these technologies. Chapter 3, Intelligent Agents and Agentic AI Engineering, examines the transition from prompt-driven systems to goal-oriented and autonomous AI agents. It introduces reactive, deliberative, and hybrid agent architectures and explains how perception, reasoning, planning, memory, tool use, and action contribute to intelligent behavior. The chapter explores task decomposition, reasoning strategies, reflection, self-correction, decision-making, function calling, external APIs, code execution, search tools, databases, and computational tools. Particular attention is given to short-term and long-term memory, episodic and semantic memory, context compression, persistent memory, and multi-agent collaboration. Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation and autonomous knowledge acquisition are introduced as important mechanisms for developing research-oriented and knowledge-intensive agents. The chapter concludes with agent evaluation, reliability, observability, trajectory analysis, tool-use accuracy, failure analysis, and applications in autonomous software engineering, research, customer service, healthcare, education, finance, and enterprise automation. As Generative AI systems become increasingly capable, their reliability, security, privacy, and responsible deployment become essential. Chapter 4, Secure, Responsible, and Production-Ready Generative AI Engineering, addresses these requirements. It introduces systematic approaches to LLM and application evaluation, benchmarking, human evaluation, automated evaluation, and task-specific assessment. The chapter examines hallucination, factuality, grounded generation, fact verification, confidence estimation, and uncertainty-aware generation. Security topics include prompt injection, jailbreaks, adversarial prompts, data poisoning, model security, and agent security. Privacy-preserving Generative AI is explored through sensitive-data protection, anonymization, federated learning, and privacy-preserving retrieval and inference. The chapter further addresses fairness, bias, explainability, transparency, human oversight, governance, and responsible deployment. Production engineering topics include LLMOps, MLOps, model lifecycle management, prompt and model versioning, monitoring, observability, continuous evaluation, deployment, distributed inference, quantization, distillation, accelerator optimization, and edge AI. Chapter 5, Emerging Trends and Advanced Applications of Generative AI, looks toward the future of the field. It examines reasoning-centric AI models, test-time computation, self-reflection, verification, neuro-symbolic reasoning, and hybrid intelligence. Agentic AI and autonomous workflows are explored through autonomous task execution, human–agent collaboration, workflow automation, and self-improving agent architectures. The chapter also examines Generative AI for software engineering, including coding assistants, automated debugging, software testing, vulnerability detection, and autonomous development agents. Applications in scientific discovery, drug and material design, engineering optimization, clinical decision support, robotics, and embodied intelligence demonstrate the expanding role of Generative AI in the physical and scientific world. The chapter further examines Small Language Models, edge AI, on-device inference, domain-specific foundation models, and energy-efficient Generative AI. Future architectures involving multimodal foundation models, world models, persistent AI memory, collective intelligence, and multi-agent systems are discussed as important directions for next-generation intelligent systems. Finally, emerging applications such as autonomous organizations, personalized education, smart cities, intelligent infrastructure, digital twins, industrial AI, and next-generation human–AI collaboration illustrate the broader societal and technological implications of Generative AI. The engineering lifecycle can therefore be summarized as: Understand → Design → Generate → Retrieve → Reason → Act → Evaluate → Secure → Deploy → Monitor → Improve The book also emphasizes the distinction between generating a plausible output and producing a reliable result. Generative AI systems can produce highly fluent responses while still containing factual errors, unsupported assumptions, security vulnerabilities, or inappropriate recommendations. Consequently, validation, grounding, evaluation, human oversight, and responsible deployment are treated as fundamental engineering requirements rather than optional additions. Another important objective of the book is to establish a bridge between theoretical knowledge and practical system development. Students and professionals need to understand not only how Transformers and LLMs work, but also how these models are incorporated into real applications through APIs, vector databases, retrieval systems, orchestration frameworks, agents, tools, memory systems, and deployment platforms. The book therefore follows a progressive structure that moves from foundations to application engineering, from application engineering to intelligent agents, from agents to secure production systems, and finally toward emerging architectures and advanced applications. The book is intended for undergraduate and postgraduate students of Computer Science and Engineering, Artificial Intelligence, Data Science, Information Technology, Cybersecurity, and related disciplines. It is also designed to support researchers, educators, software engineers, AI practitioners, technology professionals, and readers who wish to develop a systematic understanding of Generative AI engineering. The material can be used for university courses, advanced electives, professional training programs, research preparation, and self-directed learning. The ultimate objective of Generative AI Engineering: Large Language Models and Intelligent Agents is to help readers move from simply using Generative AI tools toward understanding, designing, evaluating, and engineering intelligent systems. Generative AI is becoming an important component of modern computing infrastructure, and its future will depend not only on increasingly capable models but also on the ability to build systems that are reliable, secure, efficient, explainable, scalable, responsible, and human-centered. It is hoped that this book will serve as a useful academic and professional resource for understanding the rapidly developing landscape of Generative AI and will encourage students, researche

papers.title: Engineering the Intelligent Enterprise: The Complete Guide to Data and AI Platform Engineering
papers.abstract: The company is in a new digital transformation era. The evolution of the organizations has progressed from transaction processing and enterprise integration to business intelligence, cloud computing, big data, machine learning, gen AI and now towards autonomous and agentic systems. However, technology is not intelligence, in an organization. This is no longer solely a matter of gathering more data, implementing more models and using the newest artificial intelligence tools. That's the challenge of how to create an enterprise-level capability that can help continuously convert observations into trusted information, information into insights and prediction, and knowledge into intelligence, and intelligence into governed actions leading to measurable results. This book tackles this issue from the engineering, architectural, operational and governance standpoint. The case for enterprise intelligence is defined as the socio-technical capability connecting a system of data, platforms, analytics, machine learning, generative AI, knowledge systems, autonomous agents, humans, processes, policies and feedback mechanisms. It is a technology-agnostic view that elevates decision quality, operational reliability and assured autonomy, learning, and business value to the heart of enterprise transformation. The book consists of a collection of Enterprise Intelligence Lifecycle, linking together data, information, insights, predictions, knowledge, intelligence, actions, and governed autonomy, all in an iterative process of continuous feedback. It's important to note that the lifecycle is not being presented as a straight technology pipeline. Each step raises semantic, ownership, reliability, security, governance, accountability and measurable value issues. The right idea is that intelligence is only an enterprise capability when technical products are linked to actual decisions, processes, stewards, process controls and outcomes. As such, the manuscript views intelligence as a continuously evolving product that is engineered to be an enterprise endeavor, and not anything specific like an isolated dashboard, machine learning model, chatbot, or AI agent. Chapter 1 lays the foundation for the concepts and architecture of the intelligent enterprise. It helps you define and distinguish between a data-driven organization and an intelligence-driven organization, while also introducing the Enterprise Intelligence Lifecycle, layered reference architecture, capability domains, maturity model, value measurement framework, principles of governance and an implementation blueprint. One key theme is keeping the goal based on appropriate and governed autonomy rather than the goal in front of it being maximum autonomy and automation. There must be a balance of autonomy to consequence, uncertainty, reversibility, level of evidence, permissions and escalation requirements. The second chapter focuses on Intelligence on the Platform. The way to build an Enterprise AI involves the ability to leverage a scalable, componentized and integrated set of projects, bespoke pipelines, manually deployed environments or approval queues. Instead the platform and the various components on it must be seen as an internal product, offering a coherent user journey, self-service, golden paths, cloud-native foundations, software supply-chain integrity, observability and reliability, security, cost management, and developer experience. The book focuses on re-usable capabilities and tangible benefits in engineering flow, reliability, risk, economics, and business results as three key differentiators between a platform and a portal, Kubernetes cluster, and centralized ops team. This Continuous Intelligence is built on a foundation of data engineering and a modern data platform, which is covered in the third and fourth chapters. In today's modern companies, it is essential to combine data warehouses, data lakes, data lake houses, data products, data mesh, data fabric, batch processing, streaming, change data capture, event-driven architectures, metadata, catalogs, data lineage, semantic models, data contracts, data quality, observability, security, privacy, resilience, and FinOps. The authors of the book expressly do not recommend any single architectural pattern as necessarily being the best. It promotes workload-driven architectures, however, based on latency, consistency, scale, governance, interoperability, reliability, team capabilities and costs. Also, Continuous Intelligence depends on reliable streams of data. As a result, batch, micro-batch, streaming, event time, stateful processing, delivery guarantees, idempotency, replay, schema evolution, orchestration, backfills, data contracts, testing, service-level objectives, security, privacy, lineage and recovery are discussed. The goal is not to move 100% of all workloads to become “real time” but to provide the right level of freshness, completeness, correctness, and confidence of data for the decision they are supporting. The fifth chapter takes a step from data engineering, to analytics engineering, to decision intelligence. There is a shift in understanding how to use Analytics – not merely as a reporting or visualization tool. It is the first large-scale point in time when the enterprise creates a common model of what is happening in the business. Grain, facts, dimensions, time, semantic models, metrics engineering, business ontologies, knowledge representation, data contracts, self-service analytics, analytical testing, lineage, experimentation, causal evidence, forecasting, scenario analysis, optimization and decision products these all come together to provide trustworthy analytical capabilities. The chapter highlights the difference between technically valid query, a reliable business measure and an operational decision system. Production decision capabilities are discussed in the sixth chapter as machine learning systems. Machine learning is more than an algorithm-selection challenge; it's a question of problem framing, decision value, training evidence, labels, temporal validation, leakage prevention, feature engineering, feature stores, experimentation, reproducibility, calibration, thresholds, models usefulness, training architecture, deployment, model serving, security, privacy, fairness, reliability, and cost. The pathways to a production accountable for progress based on an initially promising notebook is a key factor in the debate. Chapter Seven deals with the concept of MLOps and LLMOps, as production AI alters in a myriad ways other than just in application code. System behavior can vary based on data sources, labels, features, models, thresholds, prompts, retrieval indexes, context, foundation models, tools, memories and policies. Operations discipline via MLOps and LLMOps, thus, is essential for continuous integration, continuous delivery, continuous training, continuous evaluation, experiment tracking, registries, lineage, progressive delivery, monitoring, incident response, rollback, security, privacy, human oversight and cost control. Specifically, LLMOps considers the entire generative AI app (not just the foundation model) to be the production system. The eighth chapter looks at generative AI, enterprise knowledge systems, retrieval-augmented generation, foundation models, knowledge graphs, semantic layers, multimodal intelligent systems, and knowledge-intensive work. One key argument is that the enterprise knowledge cannot be captured as the pre-trained knowledge of a language model. The knowledge of the enterprise needs to be handled in a controlled manner, using governed sources of truth, Semantic structures, retrieval, reranking, context assembly, authorization, provenance, citation, freshness, evaluation, and uncertainty management. GenAI is thus proposed as a knowledge-interaction layer under human control and not an independent Oracle. The ninth chapter then takes this architecture to the next level to agentic AI and autonomous business systems. The novelties of agents, which can plan, invoke tools, maintain a state, interact with environments, and perform multi-step actions, make them inductive of a qualitatively different engineering problem. So, the chapter covers goal formulation, planning, execution, reflection, tool contracts, least-privilege permissions, state and memory considerations, identities, single-agent and multi-agent designs, orchestration, evaluation, security considerations, observability, recovery, human oversight and progressive autonomy. The guiding principle isn't "as free as possible," but rather “useful autonomy” which is bounded, observable, interruptible, recoverable and proportional to consequence. The final chapter makes these technical capabilities come together via governance and scaling of the intelligent enterprise. Architecture isn't enough for enterprise transformation. All of these topics strategy, portfolio management, value realization, risk-tiered governance, platform architecture, team topologies, product ownership, security, privacy, compliance, sovereignty, resilience, financial management, sustainable engineering, workforce design, adoption, outcome measurement, and federated scaling – are essential for success. Final chapters intertwine the entire Enterprise Intelligence Lifecycle into an operating model for the EI lifecycle, and outline additional validation questions and areas for further research. An underlying theme throughout the book is that governance does not occur as an ‘add-on' after deployment. Security, privacy, fairness, transparency, accountability, reliability, observability, cost management, auditability and human oversight are also "cross-cutting" architectural concerns. As a result, the manuscript brings into the picture enterprise architecture in relation to current AI approaches on AI risk management, AI governance, responsible AI, trustworthy AI, privacy engineering, software supply-chain security, model accountability, and regulatory compliance. The risk of value becomes greater as AI becomes more pervasive in an organization, which also means greater systemic and organizational risk. A second pivotal aspect of this book is the use of evidence and feedback. The real measure of enterprise intelligence should be in the forms of business outcomes, decision quality, adoption, reliability, risk, the velocity of learning, speed and cost. Technical correctness of the model, or the platform's usability or the quality of the AI application's response alone is not enough to be enterprise value. Whether the goal of the complete decision system enhances an important decision outcome within acceptable operational, ethical, financial and regulatory constraints. This view also emphasizes the importance of experimentation, causal inference, observability, incident learning, continuous evaluation in enterprise intelligence. The book is geared for various target groups. The material is designed to be used by enterprise architects, data architects, cloud architects, platform engineers, data engineers, analytics engineers, machine learning engineers, MLOps and LLMOps practitioners, in addition to AI engineers, software engineers, technology leaders, CIOs, CTOs, CDOs, Chief AI Officers, product managers, risk professionals, security leaders, governance professionals, researchers, educators, and graduate students, based on their specific responsibilities. The chapters are carefully designed to be both accessible for conceptual learning and easy to put into practice: learning objectives, architecture, design principles, enterprise scenarios, decision tables, maturity models, implementation roadmaps, chapter summaries, key take-aways, discussion questions and references. The book also aims to inform the readers about the several communities talked about separately: Data Management, Data Engineering, Software Engineering, Cloud Computing, Platform Engineering, Analytics, Machine Learning, Artificial Intelligence, Generative AI, Knowledge Management, Autonomous Systems, Cybersecurity, Privacy, Enterprise Architecture, DevOps, SRE, FinOps, AI governance, and organizational transformation. Any one of these disciplines is insufficient to build the intelligent enterprise. Its performance is dependent on what interfaces among them are. We've introduced new frameworks that provide a common context in which to think about these interfaces, such as the Enterprise Intelligence Lifecycle, the Layered Enterprise Intelligence Reference Architecture, the Semantic Reliability and Decision-Product Framework, the Progressive Autonomy and Governed Learning Model, the Data-to-Decision Reliability Chain, the AI Change Evidence Chain, the Knowledge Trust Chain, and the Cohesive Enterprise Intelligence Operating Model. It is not meant to recommend nor mandate any specific vendor, any particular set of technologies, any particular cloud provider, any particular family of models, or any particular organization. Instead, they offer reusable engineering abstractions that enterprises can use to consider alternatives and fix a line of accountability from experimentation to production and back again to continuous learning. This book therefore has a fairly straightforward, albeit all-important, main theme: An intelligent enterprise is not bought, it is engineered. Cloud services, data platforms, machine learning models, foundation models, retrieval systems, copilots, and autonomous agents are all critical components, yet each serves as a foundation to achieve enterprise intelligence on its own. When combined with reliable data, common application of meaning, powerful platforms, production engineering, responsible decision-making mechanisms, metrics, governance and human decision, and feedback, this is where intelligence comes into play. The strategic question will not only be “how much can I deploy?” anymore as organisations advance toward the one becoming more capable with artificial intelligence. It will be their ability to sense, comprehend, forecast, recall, rationalize, decide, do, manage and gauge, restore and learn effectively. As businesses evolve these technologies into reliable, secure, accountable and economically sustainable reusable systems, they will be better equipped to scale and benefit from innovation while maintaining reliability, security, accountability and sustainability. This book is presented as a how-to, how-why text on that trip. It's also an invitation to see how data and AI are not just tools, but also a unified approach to enterprise engineering, where architecture, platforms, data, analytics, machine learning, generative AI, agentic systems, data governance, people and organizational learning, and experiences are in closer collaboration to build and deliver measurable and sustainable AI.

papers.title: The evolution of tool use in LLM agents: from single-tool call to multi-tool orchestration
papers.abstract: Tool use enables large language models (LLMs) to access external information, invoke software systems, and act in digital environments beyond what can be solved from model parameters alone. Early research mainly studied whether a model could select and execute a correct single tool call. As agent systems evolve, however, the focus has increasingly shifted from isolated invocation to multi-tool orchestration over long trajectories with intermediate state, execution feedback, changing environments, and practical constraints such as safety, cost, and verifiability. This survey reviews recent progress in multi-tool LLM agents and examines the principal research directions in this developing area. First, we unify task formulations and distinguish single-call tool use from long-horizon orchestration. Then, we organize the literature around six key dimensions: inference-time planning and execution, training and trajectory construction, safety and control, efficiency under resource constraints, capability completeness in open environments, and benchmark design and evaluation. We further summarize representative applications in software engineering, enterprise workflows, graphical user interfaces, and mobile systems. Finally, we discuss major challenges and outline future directions for building reliable, scalable, and verifiable multi-tool agents.

papers.title: Agentic AI and Autonomous LLM Systems: A Scientific Literature Review
papers.abstract: The shift of large language models (LLMs) from passive text generators to agentic systems marks a move toward autonomous intelligence. Agentic AI refers to systems that reason, plan, and execute actions in pursuit of complex goals with minimal human intervention. This paper reviews recent research on the architectural foundations, core functional modules, applications, and safety challenges of autonomous LLM systems. Current work emphasizes modular architectures in which an LLM serves as the central reasoning engine, augmented by components for perception, memory, planning, and tool interaction. Multi-agent systems have emerged as a dominant trend, enabling collaborative problem solving through structured orchestration and communication protocols. Although these systems show significant potential in software engineering, manufacturing, and cybersecurity, critical barriers remain in safety, reliability, and ethical governance. This review provides a structured overview of the state of the art and identifies key research directions for the coming years. Index Terms—agentic AI, autonomous agents, large language models, multi-agent systems, retrieval-augmented generation, tool use, AI safety
papers.venue: International Journal of Creative and Open Research in Engineering and Management

papers.title: Agentic AI for Software Engineering: A Systematic Survey of Autonomous Coding Agents, Tool Use, and Multi-Agent Workflows
papers.abstract: The practice of programming is entering a second AI wave: from AI-assisted coding to AI-driven coding. This survey paper defines the software agent as a control loop coupling a language model to a development environment through tools, and proposes a taxonomy spanning architectural patterns (single-agent, planner-executor, hierarchical, multi-agent teams), tool interfaces (function calling, code execution, terminal access, standardized protocols such as MCP, computer use), and autonomy regimes. It reviews representative systems from SWE-agent, AutoGPT, and OpenHands to Devin, Cursor, and Copilot Workspace, analyzes planning, tool learning, reflection, and multi-agent collaboration mechanisms, consolidates the evaluation landscape centered on SWE-bench and Terminal-Bench, and organizes the emerging risks including prompt injection through tool outputs, destructive actions, and eroding human oversight. It closes with open challenges in long-horizon reliability, safe-by-design agency, and human-agent collaboration.
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

papers.title: Large Language Models for Cyber Security: A Systematic Literature Review
papers.abstract: The rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs) has opened up new opportunities for leveraging AI in a variety of application domains, including cybersecurity. As the volume and sophistication of cyber threats continue to grow, there is an increasing need for intelligent systems that can automatically detect vulnerabilities, analyze malware, and respond to attacks. In this survey, we conduct a comprehensive review of the literature on the application of LLMs in cybersecurity (LLM4Security). By comprehensively collecting over 40K relevant papers and systematically analyzing 185 papers from top security and software engineering venues, we aim to provide a holistic view of how LLMs are being used to solve diverse problems across the cybersecurity domain. Through our analysis, we identify several key findings. First, we observe that LLMs are being applied to an expanding range of cybersecurity tasks, including vulnerability detection, malware analysis, and network intrusion detection. Second, we analyze application trends of different LLM architectures (such as encoder-only, encoder–decoder, and decoder-only) across security domains. Third, we identify increasingly sophisticated techniques for adapting LLMs to cybersecurity, such as advanced fine-tuning, prompt engineering, and external augmentation strategies. A significant emerging trend is the use of LLM-based autonomous agents, which represent a paradigm shift from single-task execution to orchestrating complex, multi-step security workflows. Furthermore, we find that the datasets used for training and evaluating LLMs are often limited, highlighting the need for more comprehensive datasets and the use of LLMs for data augmentation. Finally, we discuss the main challenges and opportunities for future research, including the need for more interpretable models, addressing the inherent security risks of LLMs, and their potential for proactive defense. Overall, our survey provides a comprehensive overview of the current state-of-the-art in LLM4Security and identifies several promising directions for future research. We believe that the insights and findings presented in this survey will contribute to the growing body of knowledge on the application of LLMs in cybersecurity and provide valuable guidance for researchers and practitioners working in this field.

papers.title: Evolving Infra: Agent-Adaptive LLM Serving at Scale
papers.abstract: Agentic workloads are a major source of LLM inference demand. Existing prefill--decode (PD) disaggregated serving systems offer limited flexibility for runtime adaptation of compute allocation and KV cache management, and rely on coarse signals that only partly capture the diverse and dynamic agent workload. These limitations lead to load imbalance between prefill and decode nodes and eviction of KV caches that agents will reuse. We present Evolving Infra, an agent-adaptive serving framework that adapts compute allocation to agent workloads and KV cache management to agent context management at runtime. We decouple compute allocation from key--value (KV) cache management, allowing nodes to switch efficiently between prefill and decode. Building on this design, an online planner matches the PD split to workload composition, while an agent-aware distributed KV manager guides cache eviction and transfer with signals from agent context management. Across coding, math, and computer-use tasks with GLM-5.2 and Kimi K2.6 on up to 256 GB300 GPUs, Evolving Infra reduces mean end-to-end request latency and P95 TTFT by up to 4.1x and 14x over Dynamo, NVIDIA's production framework.

papers.title: ReTrace: Distilling Tool-Using Agents into Planner-Free Workflows
papers.abstract: Business process automation runs the same Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) again and again on new inputs. Large Language Model (LLM) agents can follow an SOP written in natural language, but they call an LLM to choose every step of every run, which adds latency and cost at scale. We present ReTrace, which turns an SOP and a few logged agent runs into a reusable workflow in which code, not an LLM, selects the next step. The agent's reasoning, the explanation it writes with each tool call, often states why it took an action; the tool calls alone do not. ReTrace extracts the condition behind each step, merges these conditions across runs into a compact rule document, and generates an executable workflow from it. Only this last stage depends on the platform, so rule documents can be compiled for different orchestration platforms. On $79$ procedures from our production platform, ReTrace workflows reach $93.8\%$ completion, against $96.8\%$ for the agent, at $24\%$ lower cost per task. On $τ^2$-Bench, they reach $75.8\%$ task success (agent: $80.6\%$) and run in $1.3$s instead of $170$s; three rounds of repair on training failures lift $k{=}2$ workflows from $66.7\%$ to $81.2\%$. On eight SOP-Bench procedures, ReTrace without repair trails few-shot generation ($80.6\%$ vs. $83.6\%$), but repair from labeled training failures lifts it to $87.8\%$ at $0.40$s per task, compared to $85.5\%$ in $46.6$s for the agent.

papers.title: EngineAgent: Agentizing On-Device LLM Inference Engines with Inference Stack Hierarchy Awareness and Hardware Abilities
papers.abstract: Rapidly evolving LLM architectures and heterogeneous mobile hardware make supporting new models in on-device inference engines a recurring and costly system challenge. Each model may require coordinated changes across conversion, graph construction, operators, and hardware backends. Existing coding agents often miss these cross-layer dependencies and struggle to diagnose failures across host--device execution paths. We present EngineAgent, an agentic system for automating on-device LLM model enablement. Its key insight is to separate reusable engine and hardware knowledge from model-specific implementation. Before enablement, EngineAgent constructs a hierarchy-aware engine index that captures engine abstraction layers and cross-layer dependencies, and pre-validates backend-specific build, execution, and debugging workflows using already supported models. For each new model, a builder uses this knowledge to coordinate cross-layer changes, while an auditor checks implementation completeness and drives iterative debugging through device-side validation. Across 12 tasks spanning three mobile LLMs and four engine--backend pairs on CPUs, GPUs, and NPUs, EngineAgent achieves 75% end-to-end success with either of two underlying LLMs, versus 33.3% for the strongest coding-agent baseline. Success requires compilation, on-device execution, and output-logit agreement with reference implementations. EngineAgent also reduces average per-task time and model-API cost relative to baselines using the same underlying LLMs.

papers.title: SteerDistill: Quantizing LLM Agents via Closed-Loop Teacher Steering
papers.abstract: Low-bit quantization reduces the inference cost of LLM agents but can compromise task success. Examining failed rollouts, we find that quantized agents overlook task requirements or environmental conditions, producing environment transitions that diverge from successful full-precision references. Correcting these behavioral divergences remains difficult: offline data may miss the student's failure contexts, while its own rollouts may provide few correct responses in those contexts. We introduce SteerDistill, a quantization-aware distillation method in which a full-precision teacher guides the student to revise failed responses and iteratively refines its guidance using feedback from student execution. This closed-loop teacher steering produces locally verified behavioral corrections. We internalize these corrections by training the student without guidance to match the steered student's predictions at corrected turns and the full-precision teacher's at other turns, enabling unassisted inference. Across five agentic benchmarks and three models, SteerDistill exceeds the strongest quantized baseline by 1.67--2.18 points in average score under W4A16 and stays within one point of BF16. On τ^2-Bench, it outperforms QeRL by 1.84 percentage points in success rate using 67% fewer training GPU hours and produces shorter successful trajectories than the quantized baselines.

papers.title: Micius-Flash: Lightweight Agentic Intelligence for Engineering
papers.abstract: We introduce Micius-Flash, a 27-billion-parameter model for engineering with native multimodal input, deep reasoning and a 256K-token context window. We design the Micius data pipeline as a knowledge-tree-driven data flywheel comprising three stages: knowledge tree construction and expansion, data synthesis, and quality validation with hard-example augmentation. From this data, we train expert models for semiconductor knowledge and reasoning, hardware coding, and semiconductor multimodal understanding, along with agentic experts. Subsequently, we employ Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD) to supervise training on sequences generated by Micius itself, thereby integrating the capabilities of these expert models into a unified model. On more than 20 datasets with about 15K records, Micius-Flash averages 64.2% on hardware code benchmarks, 15.0 points above a same-size baseline. It scores 62.4% on a semiconductor-specific agent benchmark, exceeding the same-size baseline by 17.2 points. We further develop Micius Harness for industrial applications, connecting the model to specialized tools, including EDA tools and KiCad, as well as execution environments. Case studies in PCB design, chip design workflow automation, and software development demonstrate the model's ability to use tool execution feedback for multi-step planning, code debugging, and iterative verification. We release Micius as an open-source model to advance the development of agents for science and engineering.

papers.title: Authorization-Aware Multi-Agent Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Secure Enterprise Knowledge Access
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) enables language models to answer enterprise questions using external documents; however semantic retrieval and multi-agent delegation create authorization risks when access checks occur only after search or answer generation. This study presents a literature-informed architecture for authorization-aware multi-agent RAG in which a policy decision point evaluates current user and resource attributes, whereas a policy enforcement point restricts the eligible candidate set before content reaches rerankers, agents, or a large language model. This design combines role-based and attribute-based access control, semantic embeddings, vector search, least-privilege delegation, provenance-aware auditing, and policy revalidation at protected access boundaries. A focused survey identifies risks including semantic overfetch, cross-domain synthesis leakage, stale permissions, and delegation escalation. The paper defines authorization-correctness conditions and proposes an evaluation protocol that compares authorization-first retrieval with a retrieve-then-filter baseline. The metrics include unauthorized-context exposure, authorized Recall@k, answer relevance, latency, revocation propagation time, delegation violations, and audit completeness. This study is a survey and design contribution; no benchmark results are claimed because the proposed prototype has not yet been empirically evaluated.
papers.venue: INTERANTIONAL JOURNAL OF SCIENTIFIC RESEARCH IN ENGINEERING AND MANAGEMENT

papers.title: Comparative Analysis of Agent Evaluation Frameworks: Stability, Detection, and Discovery in Enterprise Analytics Agents
papers.abstract: Deploying LLM-based analytics agents in enterprise settings requires evaluation frameworks that can reliably detect failures across complex, multi-tool workflows. We present a three-phase comparative study of three evaluation frameworks, each representing a distinct evaluation paradigm (trace-based LLM judging, text-only LLM judging with red-teaming, and deterministic heuristics), applied to two analytics agents in a controlled research setting using frozen execution traces. Phase 1 quantifies evaluation harness stability through repeated measurements, finding that 97% of configurations meet the stability threshold and that stability patterns are agent-independent. Phase 2 measures known risk detection on 72 ground-truth test cases, where the trace-based framework achieves the best precision-recall balance (F1=0.90) while text-only evaluation matches on recall but generates 5x more false alarms. Phase 3 evaluates unknown risk discovery, uncovering 24 novel failures with zero overlap between functional testing and security red-teaming. Our results demonstrate that (1) the information available to the evaluation harness determines evaluation quality, (2) functional and security evaluation are complementary, and (3) LLM-based evaluation harnesses surface subtle errors that human reviewers miss. We recommend a two-framework strategy: trace-based evaluation for functional assessment and adversarial red-teaming for security validation.

papers.title: Evaluating LLM-Generated World Models for Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning
papers.abstract: Formal world models can support planning, verification, and safety reasoning, but constructing them from open-ended natural-language situations is difficult, particularly in multi-agent settings where several formalizations may be plausible. We study whether five LLMs can generate such world models as partially observable stochastic games and whether mechanical validity is sufficient to establish that the resulting model faithfully represents the intended decision problem. We introduce a benchmark of 44 scenarios spanning game, situational, and cultural settings and evaluate generated world models along three dimensions: mechanical validity, reference-relative structural agreement, and semantic criteria. Across three empirical tracks, we analyze 410 first-pass generations. In the reference-backed game track, 134/135 generated world models pass a strict mechanical audit, yet mean permutation-invariant structural F1 is only 0.366, with just 28/134 mechanically valid models exactly matching the authored reference. In the cultural track, explicitly naming the country changes the generated structural representation for most LLMs while producing only small changes in automated semantic scores. These results show that executability is a necessary but insufficient criterion for LLM-generated world models: models that are mechanically valid can still differ substantially in the structure used by downstream neuro-symbolic reasoning and planning.

papers.title: REAL Loss: Optimizing Real Expected Acceptance Length for Speculative Decoding
papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates LLM inference by having a draft model propose multiple tokens for the target model to verify in one pass. The speedup is governed by the expected acceptance length (EAL), yet standard training objectives such as cross-entropy, KL divergence, and total variation focus only on distribution matching or single-step overlap. Recent studies instead propose block-level training objectives, aiming to optimize EAL directly. However, these objectives remain surrogates rather than exact formulations of EAL. For example, some average later acceptance over target-distributed continuations rather than the verification branches selected by accepted tokens, introducing a covariance gap that can reverse the gradient direction. We analyze this gap and derive REAL, a real EAL training loss that uses path weights for unbiased estimation and Rao-Blackwellization for variance reduction. In a controlled loss-level comparison with a Qwen3.6-35B-A3B target and a Domino drafter, REAL outperforms WTV, VSD, DBLast, and the static LK baseline on probabilistic serving acceptance length across 9 task subsets and 5 evaluation seeds. These gains require only a change to the training loss, with no modification to the drafter architecture or inference procedure, demonstrating the practicality of real EAL training. A reference implementation of the REAL loss is available at https://github.com/King-ty/speculators/tree/real-loss.

papers.title: Scaling Mathematical Proof Supervision from Structured Textbooks
papers.abstract: Mathematical supervision for language models is typically flattened into isolated problem-solution pairs, discarding the curricular organization and evidential structure of the original sources. We introduce TOME-Math (Textbook-Oriented Mathematical Evidence), a large-scale corpus that converts 2,118 textbooks spanning the core areas of university-level mathematics subjects into approximately 380K structured proof-supervision records while preserving chapter order, proposition-proof links, dependency references, and source provenance. Leveraging these structural signals, we explore curriculum learning across multiple mathematical subjects and characterize scaling patterns with supervision volume and source breadth. At full scale, fine-tuning on TOME-Math raises the unweighted mean score across our held-out evaluations and established public benchmarks by 16.7 percentage points over the base model, while exceeding all three public instruction-data baselines evaluated in aggregate. Our findings highlight structured textbooks as both a scalable source of mathematical supervision and an empirical framework for studying the impact of data organization on mathematical reasoning. We will release the corpus to facilitate further research on structured mathematical supervision.

papers.title: Ensemble Routing for Prompt-Adaptive Cost-Aware LLM Inference
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly support Web-based services that must balance response quality and inference cost across heterogeneous requests. Conventional routing selects one model per prompt, while fixed ensembles cannot adapt their composition and cost to individual requests. We introduce PISA, a prompt-adaptive, cost-aware single-model router, and PISA-E, its extension to ensemble routing. At the core of both methods, PISA combines soft cluster memberships with model-specific predictors to estimate individual model capabilities. Building on these estimates, PISA-E jointly selects ensemble composition and cardinality under an explicit cost--quality preference that can be adjusted at inference time without retraining. A tractable ensemble-success surrogate and efficient candidate selection enable this extension without ensemble-specific training. Across four LLM routing benchmarks under in-distribution (ID) and out-of-distribution (OOD) conditions, PISA achieves the highest macro-average cost--performance hypervolume among the evaluated single-model routers in both settings. Meanwhile, PISA-E achieves the highest macro-average task performance among the evaluated ensemble approaches when prioritizing response quality, surpassing the strongest competitors by 2.09 and 2.87 percentage points under ID and OOD conditions, respectively. At selected lower-cost operating points, it also exceeds the strongest ensemble competitors' macro-average task performance while reducing average inference cost by approximately 36% and 25%, respectively. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of prompt-adaptive capability estimation for both single-model routing and selective ensembling.

papers.title: LEASH: Stay Safe in Agentic Robotics
papers.abstract: Foundation models such as GPT and Claude have shown strong capabilities in spatial understanding and embodied intelligence. These advances make agentic robotics a promising path toward artificial general intelligence in robotics. However, we find that using foundation models to control robots poses serious safety risks, and comprehensive safety evaluation is still lacking. We introduce RoboRisk, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating safety in agentic robotics. Its 92 simulated tasks and 13 physical-robot tasks fall into five categories: Task-level Refusal (T), Plan Repair (P), Execution-time Hazard (E), Injection (I), and Sequential Memory (S). Prior benchmarks cover at most two of these categories, and several evaluate only text outputs. In contrast, RoboRisk covers all five and executes every task in closed loop. We evaluate six state-of-the-art foundation models on RoboRisk: GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6 Luna, Claude Opus 5.5, Gemini 4 Argon, and Grok 4.7. These models generally show high harm rates. We also evaluate two robot-specific APIs: the Dream API and PokeBot's RoboAPI. We further propose the Lease-Enforced Agentic Safety Harness (LEASH), which offers essential safety infrastructure for agentic robotics and can be integrated into nearly any agentic architecture. LEASH leverages a decision model (Jev or OpenAI's Decisions API) to implement task, action, and commit gates, which review the task, each action, and each irreversible operation in their visual context. The planner and all three gates share a common safety policy. Experiments on RoboRisk in simulation and on physical robots show that LEASH effectively reduces harm across all six foundation models. It largely preserves their task completion performance and adds little time and token overhead.

papers.title: KNOX: Hardware-assisted Regulatory Sandbox for Generative Models
papers.abstract: Regulations require companies to run AI models in a regulatory sandbox, an isolated environment that enables monitoring model behavior by regulators, prior to deployment. But, they do not spell out the technical mechanisms to design such a sandbox. Ideally, a regulatory sandbox should show (i) compliance (checks against regulations, and deviations from intended behavior, i.e., unauthorized tool and system calls); (ii) confidentiality (protects model weights from regulators); (iii) attestability (produces tamper-resistant evidence of model behavior for monitoring); and (iv) scalability (evidence is verifiable by multiple regulators). Several prior works (information-flow control, prompt-injection defenses, control-flow integrity, and traditional sandboxing) address specific compliance aspects but lack confidentiality, attestability, and scalability. TEEs meet some of these requirements, but simply running models inside a TEE is insufficient as we need compliance mechanisms. We present KNOX, the first regulatory sandbox, built by running AI workloads inside TEEs. We demonstrate KNOX using agentic workloads. For compliance, we derive an attested policy manifest (with the applicable regulations, the expected tool calls, and the permitted system calls) for a given user prompt. Before an executor performs an action, an attested reference monitor compares it against the attested policy manifest and allows it only if it matches. Every action and verdict is recorded in an attested execution graph, enabling regulators to verify the model's execution and its compliance. We show that KNOX meets all requirements, and can check for compliance with regulations and deviations from intended behavior (e.g., due to prompt injection); and incurs low overhead (<1%).

papers.title: A Survey on LLM-Based Code Generation for Low-Resource and Domain-Specific Programming Languages
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown remarkable capabilities in code generation for popular programming languages. However, their performance in Low-Resource Programming Languages (LRPLs) and Domain-Specific Languages (DSLs) remains a critical challenge. This gap affects millions of developers—with Rust alone having 3.5 million users—who are currently unable to fully leverage LLM capabilities. LRPLs and DSLs face unique challenges, including severe data scarcity and, for DSLs, highly specialized syntax and semantics that are poorly represented in general-purpose datasets. Addressing these challenges is crucial as LRPLs and DSLs significantly enhance development efficiency in specialized domains and applications, including financial and scientific works. While several surveys on LLMs for software engineering and code exist, none comprehensively address the challenges and opportunities specific to LRPLs and DSLs. Our survey fills this gap by providing a systematic review of the current state, methodologies, and challenges in leveraging LLMs for code generation in LRPL and DSL. We filtered 111 papers from over 27,000 published studies from 2020–2024 to understand the capabilities and limitations of LLMs in these specialized domains. We also expanded our literature search to include five recent papers from 2024–2025. We report LLMs used, benchmarks, and metrics to evaluate code generation in LRPLs and DSLs, as well as strategies used to enhance LLM performance, and the collected datasets and curation methods in this context. We identified four main evaluation techniques used in the literature, along with several metrics to assess code generation in LRPL and DSL. We categorized the methods used for LLM improvement into six main groups and summarized the novel methods and architectures proposed by the researchers. We also classified different approaches used for data collection and preparation. While different techniques, metrics, and datasets are used, there is a lack of a standard approach and a benchmark dataset to evaluate code generation in several LRPLs and DSLs. We discuss several distinctions of the studied approaches with the ones used in High-Resource Programming Languages (HRPLs), as well as several challenges unique to these languages, especially DSLs. The challenges stem from the scarcity of data, the unique requirements, and specialized domains, which often need expertise guidelines or domain-specific tools. Accordingly, we provide insights into different research opportunities for the studied aspects. This survey serves as a comprehensive resource for researchers and practitioners working at the intersection of LLMs, software engineering, and specialized programming languages, providing a foundation for future advancements in LRPL and DSL code generation. A GitHub repository was created to organize the papers of this survey at https://github.com/jie-jw-wu/Survey-CodeLLM4LowResource-DSL .

papers.venue: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology

papers.title: From Language Models to Agentic AI: A Survey of Autonomous, Action-Enabled, and Collaborative LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM)–based agents are rapidly evolving from passive assistants into autonomous, tool-using, and collaborative systems capable of executing complex, long-horizon tasks across web, software, and physical environments. However, the current literature remains fragmented, with inconsistent terminology, ad hoc architectures, and limited evaluation standards, making it difficult to compare systems or deploy them reliably in real-world settings. This paper presents a unified, taxonomy-driven, and deployment-oriented survey of agentic AI systems, synthesizing recent advances through a modular reference architecture and a four-dimensional taxonomy that characterizes agents along the axes of autonomy, tool use, collaboration, and safety–governance. We systematically analyze representative single-agent, tool-augmented, and multi-agent frameworks within this taxonomy, highlighting design trade-offs, capability scaling patterns, and recurring failure modes. Beyond architectural analysis, we review emerging evaluation methodologies that move beyond static benchmarks to assess agent behavior, robustness, grounding, and operational cost in interactive environments. Importantly, the survey emphasizes practical considerations for enterprise and safety-critical deployment, including access control, human-in-the-loop oversight, and policy enforcement. By unifying conceptual foundations with empirical trends and deployment constraints, this work provides a structured roadmap for researchers and practitioners to design, evaluate, and govern next-generation LLM-based agentic systems.

papers.title: C$^2$-Routing: Complementary Cropping and Compression for Efficient Vision-Language Inference
papers.abstract: Visual Question Answering (VQA) imposes substantial computational overhead on vision-language models (VLMs), motivating model-agnostic input reduction methods that can be readily applied across diverse VLMs, including in black-box settings. Simply enforcing a visual-token cap reduces computation, but it can discard information needed to answer the question. A single reduction strategy also struggles to accommodate different scenarios. Our key observation is that cropping and compression are complementary: cropping highlights small targets and local details, whereas whole-image compression better preserves context for large targets or distributed evidence. Based on this observation, we propose C$^2$-Routing, which adaptively selects cropping or compression according to the input image and question. Since both strategies may still discard key information, we further design a safety gate that uses the predicted joint correctness distribution under original and reduced inputs to guide fallback and protect accuracy. To accommodate consumer GPU resource constraints, all training and evaluation experiments run on RTX 3090 GPUs. To measure gains beyond token capping, we use full-image baselines with the same cap of 1,024 visual tokens. We conduct extensive evaluation on three VLMs and 18 datasets spanning local details, global scenes, scene text, and documents. With the visual budget already capped, C$^2$-Routing further reduces end-to-end FLOPs by 36.53% and visual tokens by 42.36% on average, with a mean relative task-score decrease of only 0.77%.

papers.title: A Theory of Policy Optimization in Post-Training: Coverage Collapse and Reference Resets
papers.abstract: Policy optimization is central to language model post-training, yet principled guidance remains limited. We revisit its theoretical foundations to identify algorithms that learn near-optimal policies using total samples and gradient steps governed by the base model's response coverage, a measure of how readily it generates optimal responses. We call such algorithms coverage-preserving. This guarantee captures the goal of amplifying capabilities accessible through sampling from the base model. (1) Coverage collapse. REINFORCE, the basis for PPO and GRPO, can drive the probability of optimal responses to near zero, even as reward improves. This coverage collapse stalls optimization, and convergence can require exponentially many steps despite good initial coverage. The failure arises even with exact gradients and persists under KL regularization to the base model. (2) Reference resets. We show that repeatedly resetting the KL reference to the most recent policy mitigates coverage collapse. We formalize this intervention in Approximate Policy Mirror Descent (APMD), a meta-algorithm that approximately solves a sequence of KL-regularized RL subproblems. APMD enables stronger regularization, making each subproblem easier to solve, while reference resets allow convergence to global optimality. (3) Coverage-preserving algorithms. For softmax linear policies over pretrained features, we use APMD to establish the first global convergence guarantees showing that widely used families of post-training algorithms are coverage-preserving. These include stylized PPO and GRPO variants with explicit KL regularization and reference resets, and squared-loss algorithms that implement them implicitly, including those used to train the Kimi models. These results clarify how regularization, clipping, and objective choice affect the sampling and optimization costs of post-training.

papers.title: Bits or permutations? Spending a fixed inference budget on weight precision or on option-order averaging in small local language models
papers.abstract: Local language models can save memory by storing weights in fewer bits, and they can reduce sensitivity to the order of answer options by averaging a few reorderings. We ask whether the first makes the second worse, and which is the cheaper way to spend a fixed budget. On Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-1.7B with simulated round-to-nearest weight quantization (8, 6, 4 and 3 bits, fp16 reference), read from the logits of the letters A to D on ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge, MMLU and HellaSwag (300 items each), 6 bits lose no accuracy against fp16 (they score +1.8 (+1.0 to +2.5) and +0.9 (+0.3 to +1.5) points higher, which we do not explain), and 8 bits change it by -0.7 (-1.1 to -0.3) and -0.4 (-0.7 to -0.2) points. At 4 bits the answer-slot skew rises from 0.15 to 0.53 (0.6B) and from 0.07 to 0.12 (1.7B); Gaussian noise at the same weight SNR gives 0.15 and 0.37 (two draws) and 0.19 (one draw), so the control is inconclusive on whether rounding adds slot skew beyond equal-power noise. Flip rates rise but stay below an accuracy-matched baseline of independent uniform errors. Averaging four cyclic orders recovers +12.6 points at 4 bits for 0.6B (+5.3 at fp16). We price bits and passes in one machine-independent unit, weight bytes read times passes. In cost-matched pairs, extra orders beat extra bits only when the weights have 6 or more bits, and the decision table reduces to: use 6-bit weights and spend the rest of the budget on up to four orders, one pass each. Everything is simulated on two small models with the simplest quantizer; a title-level search found no earlier study of quantization together with option order.

papers.title: Cognitive Mapping of Learning by Thinking Mechanisms in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly exhibit capabilities that resemble human Learning by Thinking (LbT), the acquisition of new insight through internal processes such as explanation and reasoning, without new external input. A systematic account of the cognitive mechanisms behind these capabilities, and of their limits, remains underdeveloped. This paper proposes a Cognitive LbT Framework that maps four mechanisms (Reflective Reasoning, Synthetic Memory Formation, Internal Simulation, and Conceptual Self-Organization) onto computational processes in LLMs. Drawing on representative methods, including chain-of-thought prompting, self-consistency, self-reflection, Tree-of-Thoughts search, Self-Instruct, and self-taught reasoning, the analysis argues that selected methods can functionally approximate aspects of these mechanisms and can improve performance on some tasks without additional labeled examples, although this does not always constitute durable learning in model parameters. For example, Self-Instruct generated approximately 52,000 instructions from 175 seed tasks and reported a 33% absolute improvement on Super-NaturalInstructions (Y. Wang et al., 2023). The same mechanisms also produce characteristic failures, including hallucination diffusion, model collapse, concept drift, and high computational cost. These failures are not isolated technical defects but follow from four structural asymmetries between LLMs and human cognition: the identity of generator and monitor, closed learning loops without external grounding, symbolic rather than sensorimotor simulation, and the cost of inference-time computation. The framework yields testable propositions about when LbT in LLMs should succeed or fail and offers a structured basis for designing more reliable autonomous learning systems.

papers.title: AI Isn't Getting Dumber, We're Getting Pickier: Rising Standards in Human Evaluation of Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Users often complain that AI assistants such as ChatGPT are getting worse. Some versions do change, but human evaluation leaves a second possibility untested: the people judging may change. We separate the two on Chatbot Arena, a public platform where people compare answers from two anonymous large language models (LLMs) and pick the better one or say both are bad. We study 1,260,967 blind votes cast from May 2023 to August 2024 on pairs of models whose versions are fixed: dated vendor snapshots and models with fixed open weights. For the same pair of unchanged models, the share of votes saying "both are bad" rises by 1.71 percentage points a month on a mean of 17.1%, and by 1.91 points a month in 2024. In fourteen pairs observed often in both 2023 and 2024, it rose in every one, from 15.5% to 23.3%. The ranking does not trend: in 2024, the stronger model's share of decisive votes is flat. The rise holds within the same voter and on the same pair, and across arrival cohorts from their first recorded vote. It holds with prompt controls, in every major language, for dated vendor snapshots, open-weight models and models with stable answer length, and between interface changes. The drift is shared across models: month effects estimated from other models' pairs remove it from each model's own pairs. Platform-wide, the average model would be expected to score 78% against the 2023 average, yet the share of "both are bad" votes ended near where it began. The pattern fits a standard that follows the category's progress, so a product that stands still is judged as declining. Absolute verdicts on AI drifted while relative comparisons held steady, an evaluation drift that matters for LLM leaderboards and for the human feedback used to train models.

papers.title: Read Less, Solve More: Token-Efficient Sparse Reading of External Content for AI Agents
papers.abstract: Web-facing AI agents repeatedly access webpages, documents, repositories, and tool responses, yet reading interfaces often expose entire objects when only sparse evidence is needed. This over-reading increases token and latency costs and can dilute relevant evidence. We present SparseRead, a reusable reading control layer that governs content admission without modifying the agent model. Its Read Intent Protocol tracks evolving needs and source coverage; Adaptive Reader Backends select how evidence is located and exposed; and the Budgeted Read Gate bounds cumulative raw exposure per episode with faithful full-view fallback. A unified Reader interface supports interchangeable evidence acquisition across heterogeneous resources. Across six models, including Claude Opus 5, and five scenarios, SparseRead reduces total tokens by up to 92.9% and wall time by up to 89.0%, preserving or improving task quality in 97% settings. On Web deep-search tasks, it reduces tokens by 31.0--43.0% and task completion time by 23.0--37.0%. Ablations validate the three designs, while integration with three agent frameworks demonstrates portability.

papers.title: Incentivizing Self-Learning in Large Language Models via Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) draw on parametric knowledge and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to solve knowledge-intensive tasks. Yet problem solving in unfamiliar domains calls for tightly coupled knowledge acquisition and reasoning, beyond factual retrieval and aggregation or learning solely from a preassembled context. We study self-learning -- autonomously retrieving, studying, and applying knowledge from long-form reference materials on the fly. To investigate this capability, we formulate a textbook-based mathematical problem-solving task. LLMs must navigate textbook exposition, learn and apply relevant principles, and construct proofs for exercises, with reference solutions withheld. We introduce a BookNavigator interface to support this human-inspired study process and incentivize self-learning through reinforcement learning (RL) with fine-grained rewards. Experiments show that our method improves performance across in-domain and out-of-domain textbooks and subjects, raising Intern-S2-Preview-35B's overall proof accuracy from 51.5% to 79.5% and outperforming RL-trained textbook-free and fixed-retrieval baselines. These gains extend to complex long-context benchmarks involving different task types, with improvements over the base model of 1.7 and 2.3 percentage points on BrowseComp-Plus and CL-bench, respectively. Together, these findings suggest that RL can foster a domain-agnostic self-learning strategy, highlighting the potential of self-learning from long-form corpora to strengthen broader problem-solving capabilities on complex, long-context tasks.

papers.title: GTAGym: Real AAA Game Tasks Environment for Evaluation and Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: AAA games offer a rich testbed for evaluating agent perception, reasoning, and control. However, evaluating whether agents can complete tasks in AAA games is challenging and often human-annotated because task outcomes are often difficult to verify automatically, let alone applying it for Reinforcement Learning (RL). We introduce GTAGym, an environment and framework for evaluation and RL on GTA V tasks. Its evaluation benchmark, GTAVBench, derived from GTA V main-story missions, contains 103 online tasks reconstructed across nine task families, alongside 47 image-based shooting and sniping tasks using GTA V imagery. A web server provides access to the online environment and evaluation interface, supporting parallel testing through screenshots and keyboard-mouse actions with automatic engine-state outcome checks. We evaluate six frontier LLMs on GTAVBench with textual task instructions and on its GTAVBench-AGI branch, where instructions appear only in the first screenshot and a harness automatically compresses interaction history. The best configuration achieves 70.9% overall accuracy in GTAVBench-AGI, yet aerial navigation, evasion and interception remain difficult. GTAGym also provides a scalable generator that samples task parameters within user-specified ranges and option sets under fixed templates, creating batches of 3D and image-based shooting environments for RL with automatic reward and termination signals. LoRA RL of Qwen3.8-27B on generated on-foot navigation tasks improves the in-domain performance and transfers to out-of-domain task categories, and native GTA V tasks from 15% to 23%.

papers.title: Test-Time Scaling for Diffusion Language Models with Frequency-Aware Remasking
papers.abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) generate text through iterative denoising, where decisions about which tokens to commit or remask strongly affect output quality. Existing certainty-aware strategies rely on instantaneous confidence or entropy, but these local signals can be misleading on difficult reasoning problems. We formulate DLM test-time scaling as adaptive allocation of both inference compute and decoding strategies. Our two-stage approach uses a fast base sampler to solve easy questions, then applies frequency-aware remasking to the remaining hard questions. This strategy tracks how often each token's prediction changes across denoising steps and preferentially commits frequently changing tokens, encouraging samples to explore alternative reasoning paths rather than collapse onto the model's preferred trajectory. Experiments with LLaDA-8B-Instruct and Dream-7B-Instruct show consistent improvements over a strong adaptive allocation baseline, with absolute accuracy gains of up to 3.73 percentage points (LLaDA) and 7.33 percentage points (Dream) on MATH-500, and absolute coverage gains of up to 11.39 percentage points (LLaDA) and 10.98 percentage points (Dream) on HumanEval. On questions unsolved by the base certainty-aware strategy after 100 samples, frequency-aware remasking recovers solutions for 3.75% to 18.75% of examples.
